title: evaluate a limit of a composite g(f(x)) by combining a verbally described graph of f with a piecewise rule for g, tracki
stem: The graph of f near x = 2 is described as follows: as x approaches 2 from either side, f(x) increases toward 3 but always stays below 3, and the point on the graph at x = 2 is (2, 5). The function g is defined by g(u) = 2u + 1 for u < 3 and g(u) = u² − 1 for u ≥ 3. What is lim(x→2) g(f(x))?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Since f(x) → 3 from below, g(f(x)) → lim(u→3−) g(u) = 2(3) + 1 = 7. The values g(3) = 8 and g(f(2)) = g(5) = 24 are not what the limit follows.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This evaluates the piece of g that applies at u = 3 itself, u² − 1 = 8, but the inputs f(x) stay below 3, so the left-hand piece of g governs the limit.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: G has different one-sided limits at u = 3, but here the inputs f(x) approach 3 only from below, so only the left-hand piece matters and the limit does exist.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This substitutes f(2) = 5 into g. The limit depends on how f(x) behaves near x = 2, not on the single value f(2).

title: evaluate a limit of a composite g(f(x)) by combining a verbally described graph of f with a piecewise rule for g, tracki (variant 1)
stem: A graph of f near x = 4 is described as follows: as x approaches 4 from either side, f(x) decreases toward −1 but always stays above −1, and the point on the graph at x = 4 is (4, 2). The function g is defined by g(u) = u + 5 for u ≤ −1 and g(u) = u² + 2 for u > −1. What is lim(x→4) g(f(x))?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: f(x) → −1 from above, so g(f(x)) → lim(u→−1+) (u² + 2) = 3.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses the piece u + 5 that applies at u = −1 itself, giving 4, but the inputs f(x) stay above −1, so the right-hand piece u² + 2 governs.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: G has a jump at u = −1, but the inputs f(x) approach −1 only from above, so only one piece matters and the limit exists.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This substitutes f(4) = 2 into g to get g(2) = 6. The limit depends on the behaviour of f near x = 4, not on the value f(4).

title: evaluate a limit of a composite g(f(x)) by combining a verbally described graph of f with a piecewise rule for g, tracki (variant 2)
stem: Near x = −3 the function f satisfies f(x) > 2 for every x ≠ −3, f(x) approaches 2 as x → −3, and f(−3) = 2. The function g is given by g(u) = (u² − 4)/(u − 2) for u ≠ 2 and g(2) = 7. What is lim(x→−3) g(f(x))?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This uses g(2) = 7. The inputs f(x) approach 2 but are never equal to 2 for x ≠ −3, so the limit follows the formula (u² − 4)/(u − 2) = u + 2, not the single value g(2).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is lim f(x), the inner limit, not the limit of g(f(x)). The inner limit must still be fed through g.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: After cancelling, g(u) = u + 2 for u ≠ 2, which is continuous near 2 in the limit sense, so the limit exists and the answer is not DNE.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: For u ≠ 2, g(u) = u + 2, and f(x) ≠ 2 near −3, so g(f(x)) = f(x) + 2 → 4.

title: evaluate a limit of a composite g(f(x)) by combining a verbally described graph of f with a piecewise rule for g, tracki (variant 3)
stem: A graph of f near x = 0 is described as follows: as x approaches 0 from either side, f(x) increases toward 1 but always stays below 1, and f(0) = 4. The function g is defined by g(u) = |u − 1|/(u − 1) for u ≠ 1. What is lim(x→0) g(f(x))?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This is the value of g for u > 1 (and also g(f(0)) = g(4) = 1). The inputs f(x) approach 1 from below, where |u − 1| = −(u − 1), so the quotient is −1.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This averages the one-sided limits −1 and 1 of g at u = 1. Limits are not averaged, and here the inputs reach 1 only from below, so only −1 matters.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: G has different one-sided limits at u = 1, but f(x) approaches 1 only from below, so only the left-hand limit is used and the limit exists.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: f(x) < 1 near 0, so |f(x) − 1| = −(f(x) − 1) and g(f(x)) = −1 for every x near 0, giving −1.

stem: A function f satisfies lim(x→2−) f(x) = 5, lim(x→2+) f(x) = −1, and f(2) = 3. What is lim(x→−2+) f(−x)?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This reads the right-hand limit of f at 2. As x → −2 from the right, −x approaches 2 from the left, so the left-hand limit 5 is the one needed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is f(2), the function value. The limit depends on the nearby values, not on the value at the point.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The two-sided limit of f at 2 does not exist, but the question asks about one side only, which is determined.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: If x → −2+, then x > −2, so −x < 2 and −x → 2−. So the limit is lim(u→2−) f(u) = 5.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The two-sided limit of f at 2 does not exist, but only one side is involved here, so the one-sided limit exists.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: x → 1− gives 3 − x → 2+, so the limit is lim(u→2+) f(u) = 0.

stem: A function f satisfies lim(x→6−) f(x) = −3, lim(x→6+) f(x) = 2, and f(6) = 1. What is lim(x→−3+) f(−2x)?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This is f(6), the function value, which does not determine the limit.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: x > −3 gives −2x < 6, so −2x → 6−. The limit is lim(u→6−) f(u) = −3.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: F has no two-sided limit at 6, but the one-sided approach here is fixed from the left, so the limit exists.

choices.label: D

title: classify discontinuities of a rational function containing an absolute value by comparing one-sided limits, distinguishi
stem: Let f(x) = |x − 3|/(x² − 9). Which of the following correctly describes the discontinuities of f?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = 3 and an infinite discontinuity at x = −3
choices.rationale: Correct: At x = 3 the one-sided limits are −1/6 and 1/6 (jump); at x = −3 the numerator is 6 and the denominator tends to 0 (infinite).

choices.label: B
choices.text: A removable discontinuity at x = 3 and an infinite discontinuity at x = −3
choices.rationale: This cancels x − 3 without handling the absolute value. For x > 3 the quotient is 1/(x + 3), but for x < 3 it is −1/(x + 3), so the one-sided limits are 1/6 and −1/6, not equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infinite discontinuities at both x = 3 and x = −3
choices.rationale: At x = 3 the factor x − 3 cancels in magnitude, leaving finite one-sided limits ±1/6. Only x = −3 makes the quotient unbounded.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = 3 and a removable discontinuity at x = −3
choices.rationale: At x = −3 the numerator is |−6| = 6, which is not 0, while the denominator tends to 0, so the quotient is unbounded rather than approaching a finite limit.

title: classify discontinuities of a rational function containing an absolute value by comparing one-sided limits, distinguishi (variant 1)
stem: Let g(x) = |x + 2|/(x² + x − 2). Which of the following correctly describes the discontinuities of g?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A removable discontinuity at x = −2 and an infinite discontinuity at x = 1
choices.rationale: Cancelling x + 2 requires |x + 2| = x + 2, true only for x > −2. For x < −2 the quotient is −1/(x − 1), so the one-sided limits 1/3 and −1/3 differ.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infinite discontinuities at both x = −2 and x = 1
choices.rationale: At x = −2 the factor x + 2 cancels in magnitude, so the one-sided limits are finite, ±1/3. Only x = 1 is an infinite discontinuity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = −2 and an infinite discontinuity at x = 1
choices.rationale: Correct: Near −2 the one-sided limits are 1/3 (left) and −1/3 (right); near 1 the numerator is 3 and the denominator tends to 0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = 1 and an infinite discontinuity at x = −2
choices.rationale: The roles are reversed. At x = 1 the numerator is 3 and the denominator tends to 0, which is infinite. At x = −2 the one-sided limits are finite and unequal, a jump.

title: classify discontinuities of a rational function containing an absolute value by comparing one-sided limits, distinguishi (variant 2)
stem: Let h(x) = |2x − 6|/(x² − 2x − 3). Which of the following correctly describes the discontinuities of h?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A removable discontinuity at x = 3 and an infinite discontinuity at x = −1
choices.rationale: The absolute value makes the quotient equal 2/(x + 1) for x > 3 but −2/(x + 1) for x < 3, so the one-sided limits at 3 are 1/2 and −1/2, which differ.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = −1 and an infinite discontinuity at x = 3
choices.rationale: At x = −1 the numerator is |−8| = 8 and the denominator tends to 0, so that point is infinite. The finite, unequal one-sided limits occur at x = 3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jump discontinuities at both x = 3 and x = −1
choices.rationale: At x = −1 the numerator is 8 and the denominator tends to 0, so the one-sided limits are unbounded, not finite and unequal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = 3 and an infinite discontinuity at x = −1
choices.rationale: Correct: At x = 3 the one-sided limits are −1/2 and 1/2; at x = −1 the numerator is 8 and the denominator tends to 0.

title: classify discontinuities of a rational function containing an absolute value by comparing one-sided limits, distinguishi (variant 3)
stem: Let q(x) = (x² − 9)/|x + 3|. Which of the following correctly describes the discontinuities of q?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only a removable discontinuity, at x = −3
choices.rationale: Cancelling x + 3 with |x + 3| works on one side only. From the left the quotient equals −(x − 3), approaching 6, from the right it equals x − 3, approaching −6, so there is no single limit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only a jump discontinuity, at x = −3, with one-sided limits 6 and −6
choices.rationale: Correct: For x < −3, q(x) = −(x − 3) → 6; for x > −3, q(x) = x − 3 → −6. The denominator is nonzero away from −3, so there is no other discontinuity.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The factor x + 3 in the numerator offsets the factor in |x + 3| in the denominator, so the quotient stays bounded near −3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jump discontinuity at x = −3 and an infinite discontinuity at x = 3
choices.rationale: The point x = 3 makes the numerator 0, not the denominator. q(3) = 0 and q is continuous there, so there is no infinite discontinuity.

title: choose the parameter that turns a discontinuity at a break point into a removable one rather than a jump, using one-side
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = 3x + 1 for x < 2, f(2) = 10, and f(x) = x² + k for x > 2, where k is a constant. For which value of k does f have a removable discontinuity at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This makes the right-hand limit 4 + k equal to f(2) = 10, but the left-hand limit is 7, so the two-sided limit still fails to exist, giving a jump.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: The left limit is 3(2) + 1 = 7. A removable discontinuity needs the right limit 4 + k = 7, so k = 3, and f(2) = 10 ≠ 7 keeps it discontinuous.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This sets k equal to the left-hand limit 7, forgetting that the right-hand limit is 2² + k = 4 + k.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This sets k equal to f(2). The right-hand limit is 4 + k, so k = 10 gives 14, which does not match the left-hand limit 7.

title: choose the parameter that turns a discontinuity at a break point into a removable one rather than a jump, using one-side (variant 1)
stem: A function g is defined by g(x) = x² + 2x for x < 1, g(1) = 0, and g(x) = kx + 5 for x > 1, where k is a constant. For which value of k does g have a removable discontinuity at x = 1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This sets kx + 5 = g(1) = 0 at x = 1. The limit must match the left-hand limit 3, not the point value.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This solves k + 5 = 3 with a sign slip, moving +5 across the equation as +5.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: The left limit is 1 + 2 = 3. A removable discontinuity needs k + 5 = 3, so k = −2, and g(1) = 0 ≠ 3.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This sets k equal to the left-hand limit 3. The right-hand limit is k(1) + 5 = k + 5.

title: choose the parameter that turns a discontinuity at a break point into a removable one rather than a jump, using one-side (variant 2)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x < 3, f(3) = 1, and f(x) = kx − 12 for x > 3, where k is a constant. For which value of k does f have a removable discontinuity at x = 3?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This sets kx − 12 equal to f(3) = 1 at x = 3. The limit from the right must equal the limit from the left, which is 6.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This sets 3k − 12 = 0, matching nothing in the problem. The left-hand limit is 6, not 0.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This stops after finding 3k = 18, forgetting to divide by 3.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: For x < 3, f(x) = x + 3 → 6. Need 3k − 12 = 6, so k = 6; f(3) = 1 ≠ 6.

title: choose the parameter that turns a discontinuity at a break point into a removable one rather than a jump, using one-side (variant 3)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = x² + 3x for x < −1, f(−1) = 5, and f(x) = k − x for x > −1, where k is a constant. For which value of k does f have a removable discontinuity at x = −1?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: The left limit is 1 − 3 = −2. Need k − (−1) = k + 1 = −2, so k = −3, and f(−1) = 5 ≠ −2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This evaluates k − x at x = −1 as k − 1 instead of k + 1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This sets k + 1 = f(−1) = 5. The right-hand limit must match the left-hand limit −2, not the point value.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This sets k equal to the left-hand limit −2, ignoring the −x term, which contributes +1 at x = −1.

title: apply the three-part definition of continuity at two junctions of a three-piece function, writing and solving two linear
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = x + 1 for x < 1, f(x) = ax + b for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, and f(x) = x² − 2 for x > 3, where a and b are constants. For what value of a is f continuous for all real x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: Continuity at 1 gives a + b = 2, at 3 gives 3a + b = 7. Subtracting gives 2a = 5.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This subtracts the two matching values (7 − 2) without dividing by the interval length 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This uses only the condition at x = 1, a + b = 2, and assumes b = 0.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This assumes b = 0 in the condition at x = 3, 3a = 7, and ignores the condition at x = 1.

title: apply the three-part definition of continuity at two junctions of a three-piece function, writing and solving two linear (variant 1)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = 2x − 1 for x < −2, f(x) = ax + b for −2 ≤ x ≤ 1, and f(x) = x² + 3 for x > 1, where a and b are constants. For what value of b is f continuous for all real x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This assumes a = 0 in the condition at x = 1, a + b = 4, and ignores the other junction.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This takes b equal to the matching value −5 at x = −2, ignoring the term −2a.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: At −2: −2a + b = −5. At 1: a + b = 4. Subtracting gives 3a = 9, a = 3, so b = 1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This takes a = 2 and uses a + b = 4 without checking the condition at x = −2.

title: apply the three-part definition of continuity at two junctions of a three-piece function, writing and solving two linear (variant 2)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = x² for x < 2, f(x) = ax + b for 2 ≤ x ≤ 4, and f(x) = 16 − x for x > 4, where a and b are constants. For what value of a is f continuous for all real x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This subtracts the matching values 12 − 4 without dividing by the interval length 2.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This assumes b = 0 in the condition at x = 4, 4a = 12, and ignores x = 2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This assumes b = 0 in the condition at x = 2, 2a = 4, and ignores x = 4.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: At 2: 2a + b = 4. At 4: 4a + b = 12. Subtracting gives 2a = 8, so a = 4 (and b = −4).

title: apply the three-part definition of continuity at two junctions of a three-piece function, writing and solving two linear (variant 3)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = x³ for x < 1, f(x) = ax + b for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, and f(x) = 12 − x² for x > 2, where a and b are constants. For what value of b is f continuous for all real x?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: At 1: a + b = 1. At 2: 2a + b = 8. Subtracting gives a = 7, so b = 1 − 7 = −6.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This finds a = 7 correctly but makes a sign error in b = 1 − a.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This assumes a = 0 in the condition at x = 1, a + b = 1.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This reports a = 7, the slope, instead of the intercept b.

stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = kx − 3 for x < 3 and f(x) = x + k² − 4 for x ≥ 3, where k is a constant. For which values of k is f continuous at x = 3?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This solves k² − 3k + 2 = 0 with the signs of the roots reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This drops the k² term from the right-hand piece, leaving 3k − 3 = −1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Correct: Left limit 3k − 3, f(3) = 3 + k² − 4 = k² − 1. Setting equal: k² − 3k + 2 = 0, so k = 1 or 2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This drops the constant 2 and solves k² − 3k = 0.

title: find the parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous at a point when the matching condition is a quadrati (variant 1)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = kx + 2 for x < 2 and f(x) = x + k² − 8 for x ≥ 2, where k is a constant. For which values of k is f continuous at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This solves k² − 2k − 8 = 0 with the signs of the roots reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Left limit 2k + 2; f(2) = 2 + k² − 8 = k² − 6. So k² − 2k − 8 = 0, giving k = 4 or k = −2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This keeps one root of k² − 2k − 8 = 0 and discards k = −2. Both roots work, since k can be any constant.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This follows from a sign slip that gives k² − 2k + 8 = 0, which has no real roots. The correct equation k² − 2k − 8 = 0 has two.

title: find the parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous at a point when the matching condition is a quadrati (variant 2)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = kx + 3 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² − 4 + k² for x ≥ 2, where k is a constant. For which values of k is f continuous at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This solves k² − 2k − 3 = 0 with the signs of the roots reversed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: Left limit 2k + 3; f(2) = 4 − 4 + k² = k². So k² − 2k − 3 = 0, giving k = 3 or k = −1.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This keeps one root and discards k = −1. Both roots work.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This follows from a sign slip that gives k² − 2k + 3 = 0, which has no real roots. The correct equation k² − 2k − 3 = 0 has two.

title: find the parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous at a point when the matching condition is a quadrati (variant 3)
stem: A function f is defined by f(x) = 3kx + 10 for x < 1 and f(x) = k²x for x ≥ 1, where k is a constant. For which values of k is f continuous at x = 1?

choices.label: D

stem: Let f(x) = √(x² − 4x)/(x − 5). On which of the following closed intervals is f continuous?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This interval contains x = 5, where the denominator is 0 and f is undefined.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: For 0 < x < 4 the radicand x² − 4x is negative, so f is undefined at most points of this interval.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The left endpoint x = 5 makes the denominator 0, so f is not defined or continuous at 5.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: x² − 4x ≥ 0 for x ≤ 0 or x ≥ 4, and x ≠ 5. On [−3, 0] f is defined and continuous (one-sided at the endpoint 0).

title: decide on which closed interval a function with a radical or logarithm and a rational factor is continuous, checking the (variant 1)
stem: Let f(x) = ln(x² − 9)/(x − 5). On which of the following closed intervals is f continuous?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: x² − 9 > 0 requires |x| > 3, and x ≠ 5. All of [−6, −4] satisfies this.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This contains x = 5, where the denominator is 0.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: The endpoint x = −3 gives ln 0, which is undefined, so f is not defined at −3 and cannot be continuous there.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: For −3 ≤ x ≤ 3 the argument x² − 9 is not positive, so f is undefined on much of this interval.

title: decide on which closed interval a function with a radical or logarithm and a rational factor is continuous, checking the (variant 2)
stem: Let f(x) = 1/(√(x − 1) − 2). On which of the following closed intervals is f continuous?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: At x = 5, √4 − 2 = 0, so the denominator vanishes and f is undefined.

title: find a horizontal asymptote of a difference of expressions that is infinity minus infinity by multiplying by the conjuga
stem: Let f(x) = x − √(x² + 4x) for x ≥ 0. As x → ∞, the graph of f approaches a horizontal asymptote. What is its equation?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This treats x − √(x² + 4x) as ∞ − ∞ = 0. The difference of two large quantities can approach any value, so the expression must be rewritten.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This multiplies by the conjugate to get −4x/(x + √(x² + 4x)) but then divides only by x, forgetting that the denominator is about 2x.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This has a sign error. x is smaller than √(x² + 4x), so the difference is negative.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: Multiplying by the conjugate gives −4x/(x + √(x² + 4x)). Dividing by x gives −4/(1 + √(1 + 4/x)) → −4/2 = −2.

choices.rationale: This reduces 6x/(√(x² + 6x) + x) by dividing by x but forgets the denominator tends to 2.

stem: Let f(x) = √(4x² + x) − 2x for x ≥ 0. As x → ∞, the graph of f approaches a horizontal asymptote. What is its equation?

stem: Let f(x) = (|x| − 6x)/(3x − 2). Which of the following gives all horizontal asymptotes of the graph of f?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This considers only x → ∞, where |x| = x. As x → −∞, |x| = −x and the limit is −7/3.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This ignores the absolute value, treating it as 0 and giving −6x/(3x) = −2.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This has a sign slip as x → −∞. The numerator becomes −x − 6x = −7x, so the limit is −7/3, not +7/3.

title: use the Intermediate Value Theorem on a table of values of a continuous function to count the zeros guaranteed, includin
stem: A function f is continuous on [0, 6]. Selected values are f(0) = 3, f(2) = −1, f(4) = −1, and f(6) = 5. Which of the following is guaranteed by the Intermediate Value Theorem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f has exactly two zeros in (0, 6)
choices.rationale: The theorem guarantees a minimum number of zeros only. Between the table values f could cross zero additional times.

choices.label: B
choices.text: f has at least three zeros in (0, 6)
choices.rationale: This counts [2, 4] as a sign change, but f(2) and f(4) are both −1, so the theorem gives no guarantee there.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f has at least two zeros in (0, 6)
choices.rationale: Correct: Sign changes occur on [0, 2] (3 to −1) and [4, 6] (−1 to 5), each giving a zero. No guarantee on [2, 4], so at least two zeros.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f has exactly one zero in (0, 6)
choices.rationale: This counts only one sign change, but there are two, on [0, 2] and on [4, 6], each of which gives a zero.

title: use the Intermediate Value Theorem on a table of values of a continuous function to count the zeros guaranteed, includin (variant 1)
stem: A sensor reading R(t) is continuous on [−3, 7]. Selected values are R(−3) = −2, R(−1) = 3, R(1) = −5, R(4) = −5, and R(7) = 1. Which is the strongest statement about the zeros of the function that the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees?

choices.label: A
choices.text: R has at least three zeros in (−3, 7)
choices.rationale: Correct: Sign changes occur on [−3, −1], [−1, 1], and [4, 7], and none on [1, 4]. That guarantees at least three zeros.

choices.label: B
choices.text: R has exactly three zeros in (−3, 7)
choices.rationale: The theorem guarantees a minimum only. R could cross zero more often between the listed times.

choices.label: C
choices.text: R has at least four zeros in (−3, 7)
choices.rationale: This counts [1, 4] as a sign change, but R(1) and R(4) are both −5, so no zero is guaranteed there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: R has at least two zeros in (−3, 7)
choices.rationale: This misses one of the three sign changes. Sign changes occur on [−3, −1], [−1, 1], and [4, 7].

title: use the Intermediate Value Theorem on a table of values of a continuous function to count the zeros guaranteed, includin (variant 2)
stem: A function f is continuous on [0, 6]. Selected values are f(0) = 3, f(2) = 0, f(4) = −2, and f(6) = 4. Which is the strongest statement about the zeros of the function that the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f has at least three zeros in [0, 6]
choices.rationale: This treats the changes 3 to 0 and 0 to −2 as separate sign changes in addition to −2 to 4. The zero at x = 2 is already one zero and counts only once.

choices.label: B
choices.text: f has exactly two zeros in [0, 6]
choices.rationale: The theorem guarantees a minimum number only; further zeros may exist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f has at least two zeros in [0, 6]
choices.rationale: Correct: f(2) = 0 is one zero. On [4, 6] the values go from −2 to 4, giving another zero by the theorem. So at least two zeros.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f has at least one zero in [0, 6]
choices.rationale: This counts only the sign change on [4, 6] and ignores that f(2) = 0 is itself a zero.

title: use the Intermediate Value Theorem on a table of values of a continuous function to count the zeros guaranteed, includin (variant 3)
stem: A function f is continuous on [−2, 8]. Selected values are f(−2) = 2, f(0) = −1, f(3) = 1, f(5) = −2, and f(8) = 3. Which is the strongest statement about the zeros of the function that the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f has at least three zeros in (−2, 8)
choices.rationale: This misses one of the four sign changes, which occur on [−2, 0], [0, 3], [3, 5], and [5, 8].

choices.label: B
choices.text: f has at least four zeros in (−2, 8)
choices.rationale: Correct: Consecutive values alternate in sign on all four intervals, giving a zero in each, so at least four zeros.

choices.label: C
choices.text: f has at least five zeros in (−2, 8)
choices.rationale: There are five table entries but only four consecutive pairs, and each pair gives at most one guaranteed zero.

choices.label: D
choices.text: f has exactly four zeros in (−2, 8)
choices.rationale: The theorem guarantees a minimum only. More zeros may exist between the listed points.

stem: Let f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 1, which is continuous for all x. For which of the following intervals do the values of f at the endpoints let the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantee a zero of f in the interval?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Here f(0) = 1 and f(3) = 1 have the same sign, so the theorem gives no guarantee, even though f does have zeros inside the interval.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Here f(1) = −1 and f(2) = −3 are both negative, so no sign change is shown.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Here f(3) = 1 and f(4) = 17 are both positive, so no sign change is shown.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: f(−1) = −3 < 0 and f(0) = 1 > 0, so the theorem guarantees a zero in (−1, 0).

stem: Let g(x) = x³ − 7x + 3, which is continuous for all x. For which of the following intervals do the values of g at the endpoints let the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantee a zero of g in the interval?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: g(2) = 8 − 14 + 3 = −3 < 0 and g(3) = 27 − 21 + 3 = 9 > 0, so there is a zero in (2, 3).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Here g(−2) = 9 and g(0) = 3 are both positive, so no sign change is shown.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Here g(1) = −3 and g(2) = −3 are both negative, so no sign change is shown.
